prompt: An FFT display’s bins are too widely spaced to study nearby tones. At the same sample rate, which change supplies more measured frequency detail?

options.text: Capture a longer stretch of the signal
options.explanation: Correct. Longer observation gives finer bin spacing and can help distinguish nearby components.
That shortens the observation and widens the bins.
Zero-padding interpolates the display but supplies no additional measured data.

options.text: Change the vertical axis to decibels
options.explanation: That changes level presentation rather than frequency spacing.

workedExample: Bin spacing depends on capture duration. A longer actual recording gives finer spacing; zero-padding only samples the same transform more densely. The chosen window also affects whether close components appear as separate peaks.

prompt: Why does `rfft` return only about half as many frequency values as the number of real input samples?

options.text: It discards the upper half of the audible bandwidth
options.explanation: It retains non-negative frequencies through Nyquist, covering the entire independent band.

options.text: The negative-frequency half mirrors the positive half for real input
options.explanation: Correct. That symmetry avoids returning redundant values; zero frequency and the even-length Nyquist endpoint are included.

options.text: It silently reduces the input sample rate
options.explanation: The transform does not change the recording’s rate.
Harmonic content is retained; this is about frequency symmetry, not harmonic selection.

workedExample: For real-valued audio, the negative-frequency half of the spectrum mirrors the positive half. `rfft` keeps the non-negative half because the other half can be inferred. For even input lengths, both zero frequency and Nyquist need their own endpoint values.

prompt: Your spectrum code uses bin index as though it were hertz. It worked for one-second captures but fails after changing capture duration. What is the repair?

options.text: Assume one bin is always one hertz
options.explanation: That special case depends on one second of actual data.

options.text: Use `np.fft.rfftfreq` with the capture length and actual sample spacing
options.explanation: Correct. It supplies the frequency for each bin under the current timing.

options.text: Multiply every magnitude by the sample rate
options.explanation: Amplitude scaling does not repair the frequency axis.

options.text: Use the number of channels as the bin spacing
options.explanation: Channel count is unrelated to the frequency axis of one transformed signal.

workedExample: A bin is an index into the transform rather than a frequency unit. Changing capture duration changes the frequency gap between indices. Generate the frequency axis from the same length and timing as the FFT input.

prompt: You zero-pad a short recording until the FFT display has closely spaced points. Can you now reliably separate two tones that the original capture could not resolve?

options.text: No; obtain a longer actual capture and choose the window appropriately
options.explanation: Correct. Extra zeroes interpolate existing information rather than add observation time.

options.text: Yes; displayed spacing is always physical resolution
options.explanation: Display interpolation and measured resolving ability differ.

options.text: Yes; padding adds new cycles of both tones
options.explanation: Zeroes contain no new observations of the signal.

options.text: No; an FFT can never distinguish nearby tones
options.explanation: A sufficiently long capture with appropriate analysis can distinguish them.

workedExample: Two close tones need enough observation time for their behaviour to be distinguished. Zero-padding draws a smoother version of the existing transform. A longer capture narrows the underlying peaks; window width and signal stability still matter.
